title: Sync vs async decode: cost & latency lab notes
content:
Purpose:
Quick working notes from the sync vs async decode experiments. Goal is to produce a short collateral draft we can use in perf reviews and product (Optimize) briefings: show where async decode buys dollars, where it hurts tail latency, and recommended knobs for conversational workloads.

Summary (TL;DR):
- Synchronous decode (single-threaded per-request decode loop, flush after token batch) gives lower p95/p99 for short-turn interactions (<= 30 tokens) at small batch sizes because it avoids stall/backpressure from multiplexing.
- Asynchronous decode (worker pool that emits tokens as produced and supports multiplexed streaming) increases throughput and GPU utilization for high concurrency, reducing $/1M tokens by ~18–32% in sustained scenarios.
- For mixed workloads (bursty short sessions + occasional long sessions), async introduces p99 inflation on short sessions during high multiplexing; mitigation by priority preemption or slot-reservation reduces p99 impact while keeping cost benefits.

Experiment setup (hardware + baseline):
- Model: open-llama-13B-quant (serving variant q4_0)
- Hardware: 8xA100-40GB (node) and single A10 test harness for single-GPU microbench
- Runtime: rdi-runtime v0.12.3 (kernel pick: nvfuser/fast-attn), with async decode patch from PR 887
- Batch sizes tested: 1, 4, 8, 16
- Session types: short-turn (mean 16 tokens), medium-turn (mean 64 tokens), long-turn (mean 256 tokens)
- Arrival patterns: sustained (1000 qps steady), bursty (Poisson bursts 10x baseline for 30s every 5min), microburst (sudden spike to 5k qps for 10s)
- Metrics collected: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (ms, end-to-end), GPU utilization (%), tokens/sec per-GPU, cost estimate ($ per 1M tokens; simple infra SRE ratecard used: $X per GPU-hour)

Key observations (raw):
1) Short-turns, low concurrency (single-GPU, test harness):
   - Sync p99: 82 ms  | Async p99: 95 ms  | Comment: async adds scheduling jitter at micro-slice boundaries
   - Sync tokens/sec: 4500  | Async tokens/sec: 4200  | Comment: small-batch overhead in async path

2) Sustained high concurrency (node-level mixed sessions, 8 GPUs):
   - Sync tokens/sec/node: 120k  | Async tokens/sec/node: 150k  | ~25% throughput uplift
   - Sync $/1M tokens: $12.1  | Async $/1M tokens: $9.4  | ~22% cost reduction (batching + better packing)
   - p95 (mixed): Sync 210 ms | Async 240 ms | p99 Sync 480 ms | Async 620 ms (note tail widening)

3) Bursty/microburst scenarios:
   - Async recovers capacity faster (multiplexing helps absorb bursts) but tail for short-turns spikes higher.
   - Sync suffers slightly higher request drop or queueing at scheduler layer when burst exceeds slot capacity.

Text charts (ascii sketches) — p99 vs offered concurrency (mixed sessions):
   offered-concurrency: 10  50  100  300  600  1200
   sync-p99(ms)       :  60  85 130 250 480 920
   async-p99(ms)      :  70 100 180 420 620 820
   note: async starts better at very high conc (1200) due to packing; but in mid-range (300–600) tail is worse because long-turns occupy encoder resources and preempt streaming tokens for shorts.

Slot packing efficiency (percent of GPU cycles doing decode work):
   batch-size: 1 4 8 16
   sync-eff(%) : 28 55 72 84
   async-eff(%) : 22 62 78 88
   takeaway: async has higher packing leverage at mid-large batch sizes; small batch ineff lost to overhead.

Cost vs SLO tradeoff (example):
- If product requires p95 <= 250ms for short-turns, sync-only configuration meets SLO at up to ~300 offered concurrency with current hw. Above that, either provision dedicated capacity (Dedicated product) or accept async with preemption/priority routing.
- If objective is minimize $/1M tokens and p95 can tolerate 300–400ms, async with adaptive priority saves ~20–30% on steady workloads.

Recommendations (practical knobs):
- Hybrid runtime mode (recommended): default to async global loop but run short-turn sessions in a low-latency fastpath (sync-like) if size < threshold and client-set low-latency flag.
  - Heuristic: fastpath if expected response tokens <= 32 and observed concurrency < 200 per-GPU.
- Priority preemption: allow short-turn fastpath to preempt one multiplex slot for the first N tokens (e.g., first 8 tokens) to reduce p99 inflation.
- Adaptive packing threshold: dynamically widen pack windows during sustained load, tighten during bursts to protect tail.
- Operator controls in Console: expose feature flags + per-customer priority policies (helps Dedicated customers tune SLO/cost).

Open questions / follow-ups (TODOs):
- Run same experiments on quantized-int8 variant (q5) — expectation: async advantage grows due to lower per-token GPU time.
- Add network jitter into harness (10–50 ms randomized) to see effect on streaming semantics.
- Validate with a multi-tenant noisy-neighbor injection (simulate low-priority training jobs sharing node)
- Metricize SDK-level backpressure (how many clients saw stalled streaming windows) and add to console UX.

Notes to self / talking points for product:
- \"Async decode is a lever: it converts utilization into dollars-saved but requires routing/policy primitives to avoid harming short interactive latencies.\"
- Present one-pager with two visuals: (1) cost vs p95 contour (iso-cost lines), (2) recommended knob matrix (fastpath threshold, preempt tokens, pack window) — I can sketch these in next pass.
